content: A woman can begin using DMPA-SC (depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, subcutaneous) within seven days of the start of her menstrual bleeding without requiring additional contraceptive protection. Alternatively, she may start at any other time if it is reasonably certain that she is not pregnant. Recommendations are also available for situations requiring additional protection, such as for women who are amenorrheic, postpartum, post-abortion, or switching from another contraceptive method. For women with regular menstrual cycles: If the first DMPA injection is given within seven days of the start of menstrual bleeding, no additional contraceptive protection is needed. If more than seven days have passed since the start of menstrual bleeding, the injection can still be given if pregnancy is reasonably ruled out. However, the woman must abstain from sex or use additional contraceptive protection for the next seven days. For amenorrheic women: The first injection can be administered at any time if pregnancy is reasonably excluded. Additional contraceptive protection or abstinence is required for seven days following the injection. For postpartum women who are breastfeeding: If less than six weeks postpartum and primarily breastfeeding, DMPA use is generally not recommended unless other methods are unavailable or unacceptable (MEC category 3). Between six weeks and six months postpartum, if the woman is amenorrheic and fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, the first injection can be given without additional contraceptive protection. If more than six weeks postpartum and menstrual cycles have returned, the injection should follow the same guidelines as for women with regular menstrual cycles. For postpartum women who are not breastfeeding: If less than 21 days postpartum, the first injection can be given without additional contraceptive protection, as ovulation is highly unlikely during this period. If 21 or more days postpartum and menstrual cycles have not returned, the injection can be given if pregnancy is reasonably excluded, but additional contraceptive protection or abstinence is required for seven days. If menstrual cycles have returned, follow the guidelines for women with regular cycles. For post-abortion women: The first injection can be administered immediately after an abortion without requiring additional contraceptive protection. For women switching from another hormonal method: If the previous method was used consistently and correctly, or if pregnancy is reasonably excluded, the first injection can be given immediately without waiting for the next menstrual period. If switching from another injectable contraceptive, the first DMPA injection should be given when the next repeat injection would have been due, with no need for additional protection. For women switching from a non-hormonal method (excluding IUDs): If the injection is given within seven days of the start of menstrual bleeding, no additional protection is needed. If more than seven days have passed, the injection can still be given if pregnancy is reasonably excluded, but additional protection or abstinence is required for seven days. For women switching from an IUD (including LNG-IUDs): If the injection is given within seven days of the start of menstrual bleeding, no additional protection is needed, and the IUD can be removed at the same time. If more than seven days have passed, the injection can be given if pregnancy is reasonably excluded. If the woman has been sexually active during this cycle, it is recommended to remove the IUD during her next menstrual period. If she has not been sexually active, she must abstain or use additional protection for seven days. Regarding examinations and tests before initiating DMPA: No mandatory tests or examinations are required for healthy women before starting DMPA. For repeat DMPA injections: Repeat injections should be administered every three months. Early injections can be given up to two weeks before the scheduled date, and late injections can be given up to four weeks after the due date without requiring additional protection. If more than four weeks late, the injection can still be given if pregnancy is reasonably excluded, but additional protection or abstinence is required for seven days. For managing menstrual abnormalities during DMPA use: Amenorrhea does not require medical treatment, and counseling is sufficient. If unacceptable, the method can be discontinued, and an alternative chosen. Spotting or light bleeding is common, especially during the first injection cycle, and is not harmful. Persistent bleeding should prompt evaluation for gynecologic issues. If no problems are found, NSAIDs may help manage the bleeding. Heavy or prolonged bleeding (lasting more than eight days or twice the usual amount) is common initially. Persistent cases should be evaluated for gynecologic issues. If unacceptable, the method can be discontinued, and an alternative chosen. Short-term treatment with NSAIDs or hormonal drugs like ethinyl estradiol may help. For progestogen-only pills (POPs): POPs can be initiated within five days of menstrual bleeding without additional protection. If started later, pregnancy must be excluded, and additional protection is needed for two days. For postpartum women, POPs can generally be initiated immediately if breastfeeding or within 21 days if not breastfeeding, without additional protection. For post-abortion women, POPs can be started immediately without additional protection. For women switching from another hormonal method, POPs can be started immediately without waiting for the next menstrual period. Follow-up for POP users: No routine annual follow-up is required, but a contact visit is recommended about three months after initiation. Women should be advised to return anytime for side effects, problems, or method changes.
